diagnostic_evidence.quote: Note that if $\mathcal{K}_F$ is an isometry, but not unitary, then the spectrum of $\mathcal{K}_F$ is the unit disc and $\spec_{\mathrm{ap}}(\mathcal{K}_F)=\mathbb{T}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|=1\}$.

issues.failure_explanation: The summary bullet for Theorem thm1 claims the algorithm 'computes the spectrum of $\mathcal{K}_F$', but the formal theorem only guarantees convergence to the approximate point spectrum $\spec_{\mathrm{ap}}(\mathcal{K}_F)$. For non-invertible measure-preserving systems in $\Omega_{\mathcal{X}}^{\alpha,m}$, $\mathcal{K}_F$ is an isometry but not unitary, and $\spec(\mathcal{K}_F)$ is the full unit disk while $\spec_{\mathrm{ap}}(\mathcal{K}_F)=\mathbb{T}$. Thus the prose claims strictly more than the formal result establishes.

failure_location.quote: there exists a deterministic learning algorithm $\Gamma_n$ that computes the spectrum of $\mathcal{K}_F$ from snapshots as $n\rightarrow\infty$

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Change 'computes the spectrum' to 'computes the approximate point spectrum' in the summary bullet.
issues.overall_effect: The summary bullet misrepresents the scope of the upper bound in thm1, suggesting the full spectrum is computed when only the approximate point spectrum is guaranteed.
issues.title: Summary overclaims computation of spectrum instead of approximate point spectrum
issues.why_classification: A short, local wording correction preserves every substantive claim and guarantee of the formal theorems.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Given $h_{n_2,j}(z,F)$ for $j=1,\ldots,n_2$, let $k$ be the largest such $j$ with $h_{n_2,j}(z,F)\in I_{n_2}^1(\epsilon)\cup I_{n_2}^2(\epsilon)$. If such a $k$ exists with $h_{n_2,k}(z,F)\in I_{n_2}^1(\epsilon)$, then $z\in \Gamma_{n_2,n_1}(F)$. Otherwise, $z\notin \Gamma_{n_2,n_1}(F)$.

issues.failure_explanation: The algorithm classifies a grid point $z$ based on which separated interval contains the last visit of the non-monotone sequence $h_{n_2,j}(z,F)$. The first claimed inclusion uses threshold $\epsilon-1/(2n_2)$, but points with $h_{n_2}(z,F)\in(\epsilon-1/n_2,\epsilon-1/(2n_2))$ lie in the gap between $I^1_{n_2}$ and $I^2_{n_2}$; the last visit to the union of intervals can land in $I^2_{n_2}$ (output 0), violating the inclusion. The second claimed inclusion $\Gamma_{n_2}(F)\subset\{z:h_{n_2}(z,F)<\epsilon\}$ can fail because points with $h_{n_2}(z,F)\in[\epsilon,\epsilon+1/(2n_2))$ can have their last visit to $I^1_{n_2}$ (output 1). The correct bounds are $\{z:h_{n_2}<\epsilon-1/n_2\}\subset\Gamma_{n_2}(F)\subset\{z:h_{n_2}\leq\epsilon+1/(2n_2)\}$.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Correct the inclusion thresholds to $\epsilon-1/n_2$ (lower) and $\epsilon+1/(2n_2)$ (upper), re-establish both inclusions from the algorithm's dependence on the last visit to the separated intervals, and choose $X_{n_2}$ accordingly to verify the $\Sigma_2$ conditions.
issues.overall_effect: The $\Sigma_2$ classification for $\Omega_{\mathcal{X}}$ in Step 2 of the proof is not established by the stated inclusions. The three-limit result for general continuous systems in thm2 depends on this step.
issues.title: Wrong inclusion bounds in proof of general upper-bound theorem
issues.why_classification: The repair requires re-optimizing the interval thresholds and re-establishing the inclusion chain (a contained nontrivial argument), but the $\Sigma_2$ result and all stated guarantees survive without new global proof architecture.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: $f:[-\pi,\pi]_{\mathrm{per}}\rightarrow [0,\pi]$ is smooth, symmetric ($f(-x)=f(x)$), $f(-\pi)=0$, $f(0)=\pi$ and non-decreasing on $[-\pi,0]$

issues.failure_explanation: For the skew product $F(x,y)=(x,y+f(x))$, any smooth function $g(x,y)=c_0(x)$ with $\int c_0=0$ satisfies $\mathcal{K}_F g=g$, so $g$ is an eigenfunction with eigenvalue $\lambda=1$ lying in $\mathrm{span}\{1\}^\perp$. Thus the claimed absence of eigenfunctions in $\mathrm{span}\{1\}^\perp$ is false. The correct statement is that the only eigenvalue is $\lambda=1$ (so $\mathrm{Sp}_{\mathrm{pp}}=\{1\}$), which is strictly weaker. Under the formal definition of $\Xi_p^{\mathrm{dec}}$ (0 iff no eigenfunctions in $\mathrm{span}\{1\}^\perp$), the value is 1 for all skew products of this form, breaking the alternation between 0 and 1 needed for the lower bound in thm:torus and thm4.

failure_location.quote: It follows that there are no eigenfunctions in the subspace $\mathrm{span}\{1\}^\perp$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Either change the definition of $\Xi_p^{\mathrm{dec}}$ to ask whether eigenvalues other than 1 exist (matching the prose intent) and restate the theorem accordingly, or construct a fundamentally different adversarial family that alternates between genuinely weakly mixing and non-weakly-mixing systems in $\Omega_p$.
issues.overall_effect: The lower bound for the decision problem $\Xi_p^{\mathrm{dec}}$ (detecting non-trivial eigenfunctions) in thm:torus and thm4 is unproven and likely false for the stated definition: the construction cannot achieve $\Xi_p^{\mathrm{dec}}=0$ for the 'odd' stages since skew products always have $\lambda=1$ eigenfunctions in $\mathrm{span}\{1\}^\perp$.
issues.title: False claim of no eigenfunctions in span{1}-perp for skew product with strictly increasing f
issues.why_classification: Every supported resolution either changes the central definition of the decision problem (altering which mathematical question is solved) or requires essentially new proof architecture with a different adversarial construction; the advertised guarantee about detecting non-trivial eigenfunctions does not survive for the stated definition.

issues.failure_explanation: The skew product $F(x,y)=(x,y+f(x))$ has rotation angle $f(x)\in[0,\pi]$, while $G(x,y)=(x,y+x)$ has rotation angle $x\in[-\pi,\pi]_{\mathrm{per}}$. Any conjugacy $h$ preserving the invariant circles must satisfy $h_1=f$ (up to winding number), but $f$ maps the circle $[-\pi,\pi]_{\mathrm{per}}$ to $[0,\pi]$ and is not injective on the circle (due to symmetry $f(-x)=f(x)$), so $f$ is not a homeomorphism of $\mathbb{T}$. Hence no $C^0$ conjugacy between $F$ and $G$ exists. The correct spectral result (the only eigenvalue is $\lambda=1$) can be proved by direct Fourier analysis in $y$.

failure_location.quote: note that the map $F$ is $C^0$ conjugate to $G(x,y)=(x,y+x)$

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the conjugacy argument with a direct Fourier analysis: expand $g(x,y)=\sum_n c_n(x)e^{iny}$ and show that $c_n(x)e^{inf(x)}=\lambda c_n(x)$ forces $c_n=0$ for $n\neq0$ (since $f$ strictly increasing makes $e^{inf(x)}$ non-constant), yielding $\mathrm{Sp}_{\mathrm{pp}}=\{1\}$.
issues.overall_effect: The proof of technical_lemma3(a) fails at its key step, leaving the spectral conclusion about the pure point spectrum ($\mathrm{Sp}_{\mathrm{pp}}=\{1\}$) unproven. Both lower bounds in thm:torus and thm4 rely on this lemma's conclusions.
issues.title: False conjugacy claim in proof of technical lemma for skew products
issues.why_classification: A contained replacement argument (direct Fourier analysis) establishes the correct spectral conclusion and preserves all guarantees that survive; no new global proof architecture is needed.
